The Panasonic NN-H98 series (often the NN-H984BF or similar models) is a popular combination microwave/grill oven. If it has stopped heating but other functions (like the clock, turntable, and grill/light) still work, this usually points to one of three main culprits: high-voltage components, safety interlocks, or power supply issues.

⚠️ WARNING: MICROWAVES CONTAIN CAPACITORS THAT CAN HOLD A DEADLY CHARGE EVEN WHEN UNPLUGGED. DO NOT OPEN THE CASE UNLESS YOU ARE QUALIFIED TO SAFELY DISCHARGE HIGH-VOLTAGE COMPONENTS. If you are not experienced with electronics repair, seek professional help.

---

### 🔍 Common Causes & Fixes (For Qualified Technicians)

#### 1. Faulty Magnetron
• Symptom: Microwave runs, turntable spins, light on, but no heat. Sometimes there’s a humming sound but no cooking.
• Fix: Test the magnetron with a multimeter:
• Check filament resistance (should be near 0Ω).
• Check for continuity between cathode and anode (should be open circuit/∞ Ω).
• If faulty, replace the magnetron. Also check the magnetron socket for arcing/burns.

#### 2. High-Voltage Capacitor or Diode Failure
• Symptom: No heating, possibly a tripped breaker or fuse blowing shortly after starting.
• Fix:
• HV Capacitor: Discharge safely and test for capacitance (~1–2 µF) and leakage. Replace if faulty.
• High-Voltage Diode: Test with a multimeter in diode mode (should show forward bias ~0.5V, reverse bias ∞). Replace if shorted or open.

#### 3. Door Switches / Interlock Failures
• Symptom: Microwave may not start at all, or starts but doesn’t heat. Sometimes the display shows an error code (e.g., "E01", "E24").
• Fix: Panasonic microwaves have multiple interlock switches. Test each switch for continuity when the door is closed. Replace any faulty switch(es).

#### 4. Thermal Fuse or Main PCB Issue
• Symptom: No power at all, or intermittent operation.
• Fix: Check the thermal fuse (usually near the magnetron or on the main board) with a multimeter for continuity. If blown, replace it—but investigate why it blew (overheating?).

#### 5. Control Board / Relay Failure
• Symptom: Random behavior, no heating, but other functions work.
• Fix: Check relays on the main PCB that control power to the magnetron. Listen for a click when starting. Replace faulty relay or entire board if needed.

---

### ✅ Quick Checks You Can Do Safely (Without Opening)

1. Reset the Microwave: Unplug it for 5–10 minutes, then plug back in. This can reset the control board.
2. Check for Error Codes: Look at the display. Panasonic often shows error codes like:
• E01/E24: Door switch issue.
• E18: Magnetron or HV circuit fault.
• E22: Temperature sensor fault.
3. Ensure Proper Ventilation: Blocked vents can cause thermal cutoffs. Clean the exhaust filters.
4. Test with a Simple Load: Place a cup of water inside and try heating for 1 minute. If it runs but doesn’t heat, it’s likely internal hardware.

---

### 🛠️ Recommendation

• If under warranty: Contact Panasonic support immediately.
• If out of warranty: Given the high-voltage risks, it’s often more cost-effective to replace a 5–7 year old microwave than to repair it, unless you’re experienced with electronics.
• DIY only if qualified: If you proceed, ensure you discharge the HV capacitor properly before touching any components.

h98 is what the screen says when it stops, the model on the back is NN-CD87KSBPQ. grill still heats fine. is it worth fixing?

The "H98" error code on your Panasonic NN-CD87KSBPQ specifically indicates a high-voltage circuit malfunction. This means the microwave’s main board has detected an issue with the components responsible for generating microwaves (magnetron, high-voltage diode, or capacitor), but it is not detecting a short circuit severe enough to blow the main fuse.

Since your grill still works fine, we know the main power supply and the door safety switches are functioning correctly. The problem is isolated strictly to the microwave generation system.

### Is it worth fixing?
Generally, no. Here is why:
• Cost vs. Value: Replacement parts (magnetron, HV diode, or capacitor) combined with labor costs often approach or exceed the price of a new entry-level combination oven.
• Complexity: Accessing these components requires disassembling the outer casing and dealing with high-voltage capacitors that hold a lethal charge even when unplugged.
• Longevity: If one HV component has failed, it is often due to age or wear on other internal parts that may fail soon after repair.

### ⚠️ Critical Safety Warning
Do not attempt to open the casing unless you are qualified. The high-voltage capacitor inside can store enough energy to kill you instantly, even if the unit has been unplugged for days. If you are not experienced with electronics repair and safe discharge procedures, do not open it.

### What You Can Do Safely (No Tools Required)
Before giving up on it completely, try these two steps to rule out false triggers:

1.  Perform a Hard Reset:
• Unplug the oven from the wall socket for at least 5–10 minutes. This allows the main PCB to fully discharge and clear any temporary electronic glitches.
• Plug it back in and try running the microwave for just 10 seconds. If the error returns immediately, it is a confirmed hardware fault.

2.  Check for Moisture or Debris:
• Look inside the oven cavity near the waveguide cover (the small mica or plastic sheet on the side wall). If it’s greasy or burnt, clean it gently with a damp cloth and mild detergent. A damaged waveguide can sometimes cause arcing that triggers error codes.

### Recommendation
If the hard reset doesn’t clear the H98 code:
• For most users: It is more cost-effective and safer to replace the unit.
• If you are handy with electronics: You could attempt a repair, but only if you have the proper tools (insulated screwdrivers, multimeter) and know how to safely discharge the high-voltage capacitor. The most common fix for H98 is replacing the high-voltage diode or the magnetron, but diagnosis requires testing these components in-circuit.

Given the age of many NN-CD series units and the safety risks involved, replacement is usually the recommended path.

Since the reset didn't clear the error and you are considering a professional repair, here is how to approach this safely and cost-effectively.

### 1. Who to Contact
You have two main options for getting an expert to look at it:

• Panasonic Authorised Service Centre: This is your best first step. They can provide the exact part numbers for the NN-CD87KSBPQ and give you a definitive quote for parts and labor. You can find the nearest centre on the Panasonic UK website or by calling their support line.
• Independent Appliance Repair Technician: Look for a local, highly-rated independent repair service. They often have lower labour rates than manufacturers. However, ensure they are comfortable working with high-voltage microwave components.

### 2. The "Sensible Repair" Reality Check
Before you book anyone, it is important to understand what the H98 code usually means in terms of cost:
• The Likely Culprits: The error points to the High-Voltage (HV) Diode, HV Capacitor, or the Magnetron.
• The Labour Cost: Because these parts are deep inside the unit and require safe discharge procedures, a technician will charge for at least 1–2 hours of labour. In the UK, this can range from £60 to £150+ depending on your location.
• Parts vs. Value: If the fault is just the diode or capacitor (which are relatively cheap parts), it might be worth it. However, if the Magnetron has failed, the total repair cost could easily exceed £200–£300, making a replacement oven more sensible.

### 3. How to Proceed
1.  Call Panasonic Support: Ask them for an estimate of the parts cost for the NN-CD87KSBPQ.
2.  Get a Quote: If you use an independent technician, describe the "H98" error and ask if they can provide a "call-out fee vs. repair cost" estimate before they come out.
3.  The Decision Point: If the quote comes in at over £150–£200 (including labour), it is often more economical to replace the unit, especially since you already have a working grill function and could potentially use that for the time being.

### Summary of Next Steps
• Do not attempt to open the casing yourself due to the lethal risk of high-voltage capacitors.
• Contact Panasonic Support first for an official diagnosis and parts pricing.
• Compare the repair quote against the current price of a new NN-CD87KSBPQ or similar model. If the repair is more than 50% of the cost of a new unit, replacement is usually the "sensible" choice.
